Reference: Aiyagari (1994); Lecture Notes 1; Lecture Notes 2

Model Setting

The paper asks how much uninsured idiosyncratic risk adds to aggregate saving. It modifies the standard growth model of Brock and Mirman (1972) by replacing the representative agent with a continuum of infinitely lived agents (of size unity) who receive idiosyncratic labor endowment shocks, cannot insure them, and can only self-insure by accumulating a single asset (capital) subject to a borrowing constraint, as in Bewley (1986). Because the shocks are purely idiosyncratic there is no aggregate uncertainty: in a steady state the interest rate, the wage, aggregate capital and the cross-section distribution of assets are constant, while each individual's assets and consumption fluctuate. Five features define the exercise: endogenous heterogeneity, aggregation, infinite horizons, a borrowing constraint, and general equilibrium (an endogenously determined interest rate).

The qualitative result is that the steady-state interest rate is necessarily below the rate of time preference, so aggregate capital and the saving rate are necessarily higher than under certainty (equivalently, complete markets). The result comes from the infinite horizon and the borrowing constraint and does not require convex marginal utility, the traditional condition for precautionary saving. The quantitative result is that the effect is modest: for moderate and empirically plausible risk aversion, variability and persistence of earnings, the aggregate saving rate rises by no more than three percentage points, and only for high variability and persistence does it rise by seven to fourteen points. The model also implies that access to asset markets is valuable to individuals (consumption variability is cut by about half), and that wealth is much more dispersed than income, although less than in the data.

The Individual's Problem

The building block is the income fluctuation problem (Schechtman and Escudero 1977): an individual facing uncertain earnings and a constant return on assets chooses consumption and assets. For the exposition, labor endowment shocks are i.i.d. over time. The individual maximizes:

E0{∑t=0∞βtU(ct)}(1)E_0\left\{\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^tU(c_t)\right\} \tag{1}E0​{t=0∑∞​βtU(ct​)}(1)

ct+at+1=wlt+(1+r)at,ct≥0,at≥−balmost surely(2)c_t+a_{t+1}=wl_t+(1+r)a_t,\qquad c_t\geq0,\qquad a_t\geq-b\quad\text{almost surely} \tag{2}ct​+at+1​=wlt​+(1+r)at​,ct​≥0,at​≥−balmost surely(2)

where ctc_tct​, ata_tat​ and ltl_tlt​ are consumption, assets and the labor endowment in period ttt, U(c)U(c)U(c) is the period utility function, β\betaβ is the utility discount factor, λ=(1−β)/β>0\lambda=(1-\beta)/\beta>0λ=(1−β)/β>0 is the rate of time preference, rrr is the return on assets, www is the wage, and bbb (if positive) is the limit on borrowing. The endowment ltl_tlt​ is i.i.d. with bounded support [lmin⁡,lmax⁡][l_{\min},l_{\max}][lmin​,lmax​] and lmin⁡>0l_{\min}>0lmin​>0.

Natural and Ad Hoc Borrowing Limits

If r<0r<0r<0 some limit on borrowing is required, because the present value of earnings is infinite and nothing would prevent a Ponzi scheme. If r>0r>0r>0, a less restrictive alternative is present value budget balance, which together with nonnegative consumption is equivalent to a period-by-period constraint:

lim⁡t→∞at(1+r)t≥0⟺at≥−wlmin⁡r(3)\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\frac{a_t}{(1+r)^t}\geq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a_t\geq-\frac{wl_{\min}}{r} \tag{3}t→∞lim​(1+r)tat​​≥0⟺at​≥−rwlmin​​(3)

The amount wlmin⁡/rwl_{\min}/rwlmin​/r is the most that the consumer can repay for sure without violating nonnegativity of consumption, so a borrowing constraint is necessarily implied by nonnegative consumption. If bbb exceeds this amount it never binds, and without loss of generality the limit can be written as:

at≥−ϕ,ϕ≡min⁡{b,wlmin⁡r} for r>0,ϕ≡b for r≤0(4)a_t\geq-\phi,\qquad\phi\equiv\min\left\{b,\frac{wl_{\min}}{r}\right\}\ \text{for }r>0,\qquad\phi\equiv b\ \text{for }r\leq0 \tag{4}at​≥−ϕ,ϕ≡min{b,rwlmin​​} for r>0,ϕ≡b for r≤0(4)

When bbb is tighter than wlmin⁡/rwl_{\min}/rwlmin​/r (for example b=0b=0b=0, no borrowing), the limit is ad hoc: it is not a consequence of present value budget balance and nonnegative consumption. The case ϕ=wlmin⁡/r\phi=wl_{\min}/rϕ=wlmin​/r with r>0r>0r>0 is the present value borrowing constraint (the natural limit).

Stationary Distribution and Aggregate Assets

Under additional assumptions, of which the key one is that the coefficient of relative risk aversion is bounded, the support of the Markov process for total resources is bounded: there is a z∗z^*z∗ such that for all zt≥z∗z_t\geq z^*zt​≥z∗, zt+1≤ztz_{t+1}\leq z_tzt+1​≤zt​ with probability one. There then exists a unique, stable stationary distribution of {zt}\{z_t\}{zt​}, which is continuous in bbb, www and rrr. Bounded risk aversion matters: with negative exponential utility there are values of rrr below λ\lambdaλ for which assets wander off to infinity. Long-run average assets, with the wage held fixed, are:

Eaw=E{A(z,b,w,r)}−ϕ(12)Ea_w=E\left\{A(z,b,w,r)\right\}-\phi \tag{12}Eaw​=E{A(z,b,w,r)}−ϕ(12)

where E{⋅}E\{\cdot\}E{⋅} is the expectation with respect to the stationary distribution of zzz. With a continuum of agents the long-run distribution of one individual is also the cross-section distribution of the population, so EawEa_wEaw​ is the aggregate asset supply of households: individual assets move stochastically while the cross-section distribution and per capita assets are constant. The function EawEa_wEaw​ is continuous in rrr but need not be monotone.

Why the Interest Rate Must Be Below the Rate of Time Preference

The most important property is that EawEa_wEaw​ tends to infinity as rrr approaches λ\lambdaλ from below, and is not finite for r≥λr\geq\lambdar≥λ. If r>λr>\lambdar>λ the consumption profile slopes upward. Formally, multiplying the Euler inequality by βt(1+r)t\beta^t(1+r)^tβt(1+r)t gives:

Et[βt+1(1+r)t+1U′(ct+1)]≤βt(1+r)tU′(ct)(13)E_t\left[\beta^{t+1}(1+r)^{t+1}U'(c_{t+1})\right]\leq\beta^t(1+r)^tU'(c_t) \tag{13}Et​[βt+1(1+r)t+1U′(ct+1​)]≤βt(1+r)tU′(ct​)(13)

so βt(1+r)tU′(ct)\beta^t(1+r)^tU'(c_t)βt(1+r)tU′(ct​) is a nonnegative supermartingale and converges almost surely to a finite random variable. Since β(1+r)>1\beta(1+r)>1β(1+r)>1, U′(ct)U'(c_t)U′(ct​) must converge to zero, so ctc_tct​, ztz_tzt​ and a^t\hat{a}_ta^t​ converge to infinity almost surely (Chamberlain and Wilson 1984). The conclusion carries over to the borderline case β(1+r)=1\beta(1+r)=1β(1+r)=1, which is where uncertainty changes the answer. The consumer then tries to keep marginal utility smooth, and holding an extra unit of the asset is costless at the margin; but a sufficiently long string of bad draws has positive probability, so smoothing is possible only with an arbitrarily large buffer. The proof is by contradiction. Write yt+1y_{t+1}yt+1​ for the part of next period's total resources that does not depend on the asset choice, with largest value ymax⁡y_{\max}ymax​. If the transition law had a finite fixed point zmax⁡z_{\max}zmax​ at lt+1=lmax⁡l_{t+1}=l_{\max}lt+1​=lmax​, the envelope condition, the first-order condition and the strict concavity of VVV would give:

V′(zmax⁡)≥Et{V′(yt+1+(1+r)A(zmax⁡))}>V′(ymax⁡+(1+r)A(zmax⁡))=V′(zmax⁡)(14)V'(z_{\max})\geq E_t\left\{V'\left(y_{t+1}+(1+r)A(z_{\max})\right)\right\}>V'\left(y_{\max}+(1+r)A(z_{\max})\right)=V'(z_{\max}) \tag{14}V′(zmax​)≥Et​{V′(yt+1​+(1+r)A(zmax​))}>V′(ymax​+(1+r)A(zmax​))=V′(zmax​)(14)

which is impossible, so the support of {zt}\{z_t\}{zt​} is unbounded.

For r<λr<\lambdar<λ (and not too far below it), EawEa_wEaw​ is higher under uncertainty than under certainty, whether U′U'U′ is convex or concave. If earnings were certain, all agents would be alike and constrained, and per capita assets would equal −ϕ-\phi−ϕ for every r<λr<\lambdar<λ. Under incomplete markets there is a distribution of agents with different histories of shocks: those with low total resources remain constrained, while those with high total resources accumulate assets beyond the constrained level simply because their current resources are high relative to average future resources. Aggregation then puts per capita assets above −ϕ-\phi−ϕ. Only if rrr is so low that even the luckiest agent wants to stay at the limit:

U′(wlmax⁡−rϕ)≥β(1+r)Et{U′(wlt+1−rϕ)}(15)U'(wl_{\max}-r\phi)\geq\beta(1+r)E_t\left\{U'(wl_{t+1}-r\phi)\right\} \tag{15}U′(wlmax​−rϕ)≥β(1+r)Et​{U′(wlt+1​−rϕ)}(15)

is everyone constrained and per capita assets the same as under certainty. If U′U'U′ is convex, a mean-preserving spread of the endowment raises the asset demand function at each ztz_tzt​ (Sibley 1975; Miller 1976), but its effect on EawEa_wEaw​ is ambiguous in theory because the stationary distribution also changes; in all computations more variability shifted EawEa_wEaw​ to the right.

Production and Capital Demand

Per capita output is f(k,1)f(k,1)f(k,1), a neoclassical production function of per capita capital kkk and per capita labor. Since shocks are idiosyncratic, per capita labor equals the expected individual endowment and is normalized to one. Capital depreciates at rate δ\deltaδ. Profit maximization requires:

r=f1(k,1)−δ,w=f2(k,1)(16)r=f_1(k,1)-\delta,\qquad w=f_2(k,1) \tag{16}r=f1​(k,1)−δ,w=f2​(k,1)(16)

The first condition defines the capital demand curve K(r)K(r)K(r), which is downward sloping, tends to infinity as rrr tends to −δ-\delta−δ and tends to zero as rrr tends to infinity. The second lets the wage be written as a decreasing function ω(r)\omega(r)ω(r). With the Cobb-Douglas form used in the quantitative part, f(k,1)=kαf(k,1)=k^{\alpha}f(k,1)=kα, these conditions imply:

K(r)=(αr+δ)11−α,ω(r)=(1−α)(αr+δ)α1−α(17)K(r)=\left(\frac{\alpha}{r+\delta}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}},\qquad\omega(r)=(1-\alpha)\left(\frac{\alpha}{r+\delta}\right)^{\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}} \tag{17}K(r)=(r+δα​)1−α1​,ω(r)=(1−α)(r+δα​)1−αα​(17)

Stationary Equilibrium

Let Ea(r)Ea(r)Ea(r) denote the value of EawEa_wEaw​ when w=ω(r)w=\omega(r)w=ω(r). A steady state is an interest rate at which the capital desired by firms equals the capital supplied by households:

K(r)=Ea(r)(18)K(r)=Ea(r) \tag{18}K(r)=Ea(r)(18)

In the diagram with rrr on the vertical axis and assets on the horizontal axis, the household curve (labelled NI, no insurance) starts at −ϕ-\phi−ϕ for low rrr, rises, and approaches the horizontal line at height λ\lambdaλ asymptotically, while K(r)K(r)K(r) slopes down. They intersect at a point ene^nen with r<λr<\lambdar<λ. Like EawEa_wEaw​, the curve Ea(r)Ea(r)Ea(r) is continuous and tends to infinity as rrr tends to λ\lambdaλ from below, but it need not be monotone: with b=0b=0b=0 and isoelastic utility a higher wage scales a^\hat{a}a^, zzz, ccc and aaa proportionally, and ω(r)\omega(r)ω(r) is decreasing. Uniqueness of the steady state is therefore not guaranteed.

Comparison with Full Insurance

With no uncertainty, or with full insurance markets, there is a representative agent with constant earnings www. For r<λr<\lambdar<λ this agent sits at the borrowing limit with assets −ϕ-\phi−ϕ, for r=λr=\lambdar=λ the agent keeps any initial holdings, and for r>λr>\lambdar>λ assets grow without bound. Desired assets are therefore a right-angled line (labelled FI): a vertical segment at −ϕ-\phi−ϕ and a horizontal segment at height λ\lambdaλ. Its intersection efe^fef with K(r)K(r)K(r) is the modified golden rule:

r=λ=1−ββ,f1(k,1)=λ+δ(19)r=\lambda=\frac{1-\beta}{\beta},\qquad f_1(k,1)=\lambda+\delta \tag{19}r=λ=β1−β​,f1​(k,1)=λ+δ(19)

Since the NI curve lies to the right of the vertical segment and below the horizontal one, ene^nen has a lower interest rate and more capital than efe^fef. There is no growth, so net saving is zero and the gross saving rate is depreciation over output, which under Cobb-Douglas depends only on the interest rate:

δkf(k,1)=δαr+δ(20)\frac{\delta k}{f(k,1)}=\frac{\delta\alpha}{r+\delta} \tag{20}f(k,1)δk​=r+δδα​(20)

It is increasing in kkk and is therefore higher under incomplete markets. The shape of Ea(r)Ea(r)Ea(r) also explains why general equilibrium limits the effect. Because household assets are extremely sensitive to rrr just below λ\lambdaλ, a partial equilibrium analysis with a fixed interest rate close to λ\lambdaλ can generate arbitrarily large precautionary saving; in general equilibrium a small fall in rrr is enough to clear the capital market, and how much saving rises is a quantitative question that depends on the elasticity of K(r)K(r)K(r). With labor-augmenting technical progress at rate ggg, a borrowing limit growing at the same rate and isoelastic utility with elasticity of marginal utility μ\muμ, the complete markets interest rate is:

r=(1+λ)(1+g)μ−1(21)r=(1+\lambda)(1+g)^{\mu}-1 \tag{21}r=(1+λ)(1+g)μ−1(21)

and the incomplete markets rate lies below it.

Role of the Borrowing Limit and Alternative Interpretations

A larger bbb shifts EawEa_wEaw​ to the left: at r=−1r=-1r=−1 assets always equal −b-b−b, and at r=0r=0r=0 the limit does not enter A(⋅)A(\cdot)A(⋅), so EawEa_wEaw​ falls one-to-one with bbb. Permitting more borrowing therefore lowers aggregate capital and moves the interest rate toward λ\lambdaλ, because borrowing substitutes for capital as a buffer. If risk with b=0b=0b=0 raises capital only a little, it raises it even less with b>0b>0b>0. Under the present value constraint with lmin⁡>0l_{\min}>0lmin​>0, EawEa_wEaw​ tends to minus infinity as rrr tends to zero, so a steady state with a positive interest rate always exists; with a fixed limit the steady-state interest rate can be negative. The individual problem can also be read as a pure exchange economy with per capita government debt ddd whose interest is financed by a lump sum tax:

ct+at+1=wlt−rd+(1+r)at,Eaw=d(22)c_t+a_{t+1}=wl_t-rd+(1+r)a_t,\qquad Ea_w=d \tag{22}ct​+at+1​=wlt​−rd+(1+r)at​,Eaw​=d(22)

where the second expression is the steady-state condition. Debt neutrality fails with a fixed borrowing limit and holds when the limit is the present value of minimum earnings net of taxes:

at≥−wlmin⁡−rdr,at∗=at−d(23)a_t\geq-\frac{wl_{\min}-rd}{r},\qquad a^*_t=a_t-d \tag{23}at​≥−rwlmin​−rd​,at∗​=at​−d(23)

since in terms of at∗a^*_tat∗​ the problem does not depend on ddd. A similar relabelling gives the optimum quantity of money model of Bewley (1983), in which interest-bearing money cannot support an interest rate arbitrarily close to λ\lambdaλ.

Specification and Parameterization

The period is one year. Technology is Cobb-Douglas and utility is of the constant relative risk aversion type:

U(c)=c1−μ−11−μ(24)U(c)=\frac{c^{1-\mu}-1}{1-\mu} \tag{24}U(c)=1−μc1−μ−1​(24)

with μ\muμ the coefficient of relative risk aversion. The values are β=0.96\beta=0.96β=0.96, α=0.36\alpha=0.36α=0.36, δ=0.08\delta=0.08δ=0.08 and μ∈{1,3,5}\mu\in\{1,3,5\}μ∈{1,3,5}, chosen to match aggregate features of the postwar United States economy. The borrowing limit is b=0b=0b=0, which gives the largest effect on saving. In the quantitative model the endowment is serially correlated, so the current shock becomes a second state variable next to total resources. The logarithm of the labor endowment follows a first-order autoregression:

log⁡(lt)=ρlog⁡(lt−1)+σ(1−ρ2)1/2ϵt,ϵt∼Normal(0,1)(25)\log(l_t)=\rho\log(l_{t-1})+\sigma(1-\rho^2)^{1/2}\epsilon_t,\qquad\epsilon_t\sim\text{Normal}(0,1) \tag{25}log(lt​)=ρlog(lt−1​)+σ(1−ρ2)1/2ϵt​,ϵt​∼Normal(0,1)(25)

with σ∈{0.2,0.4}\sigma\in\{0.2,0.4\}σ∈{0.2,0.4} and ρ∈{0,0.3,0.6,0.9}\rho\in\{0,0.3,0.6,0.9\}ρ∈{0,0.3,0.6,0.9}, so that σ\sigmaσ is the coefficient of variation of earnings and ρ\rhoρ their serial correlation. The process is approximated by a seven-state Markov chain following Tauchen (1986) and Deaton (1991). The chain reproduces the targets well: its implied values are 0.21 to 0.24 for a target σ\sigmaσ of 0.2 and 0.43 to 0.49 for a target of 0.4, and its serial correlations are 0, 0.28 to 0.3, 0.58 to 0.59 and 0.89 to 0.9. The range for σ\sigmaσ rests on panel evidence: the standard deviation of annual percentage changes in real earnings is about 40 percent (Abowd and Card 1987, 1989), and for a first-order process in log earnings yty_tyt​:

σyσg=[2(1−ρ)]−1/2(26)\frac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_g}=\left[2(1-\rho)\right]^{-1/2} \tag{26}σg​σy​​=[2(1−ρ)]−1/2(26)

where σy\sigma_yσy​ is the standard deviation of yty_tyt​ and σg\sigma_gσg​ that of yt−yt−1y_t-y_{t-1}yt​−yt−1​. This gives a coefficient of variation of 28 percent if earnings are i.i.d. and 34 percent with a serial correlation of 0.3; Heaton and Lucas (1992) estimate a serial correlation of 0.23 to 0.53 and a coefficient of variation of 0.27 to 0.4. Measurement error would lower these figures, while uninsured losses and taste shocks would raise the relevant risk.

Computation

For each of the seven endowment states, asset demand is approximated as a continuous piecewise linear function of total resources on an interval whose partition is finer at the lower end, where the binding constraint makes the function highly nonlinear, and coarser at the upper end, where it is nearly linear. The steady state is found by simulation and bisection. Start from an interest rate r1r_1r1​ close to but below λ\lambdaλ and compute the asset demand function. Simulate the Markov chain for 10,000 periods, generate the implied series of assets, and take its sample mean as EaEaEa. Compute r2r_2r2​ such that K(r2)K(r_2)K(r2​) equals this EaEaEa, replacing it by λ\lambdaλ if it exceeds λ\lambdaλ. By construction r1r_1r1​ and r2r_2r2​ lie on opposite sides of the steady-state rate r∗r^*r∗; after relabelling so that r1<r∗<r2r_1<r^*<r_2r1​<r∗<r2​, set r3=(r1+r2)/2r_3=(r_1+r_2)/2r3​=(r1​+r2​)/2 and compute EaEaEa at r3r_3r3​. If EaEaEa exceeds K(r3)K(r_3)K(r3​) then r2r_2r2​ is replaced by r3r_3r3​, otherwise r1r_1r1​ is replaced by r3r_3r3​, and the step is repeated. About ten iterations give an excellent approximation, and 20,000 draws change the results very little. The simulated series deliver means, medians, coefficients of variation, skewness (mean minus median over standard deviation), Lorenz curves and Gini coefficients for labor income, assets, net income wlt+ratwl_t+ra_twlt​+rat​, gross income (net income plus depreciation δat\delta a_tδat​), gross saving (gross income minus consumption) and consumption.

Quantitative Results

The full insurance benchmark is a net return to capital of 4.17 percent and a saving rate of 23.67 percent.

  • Low earnings variability (σ=0.2\sigma=0.2σ=0.2): the net return and saving rate are 4.1666 and 23.67 percent at ρ=0\rho=0ρ=0, μ=1\mu=1μ=1, which is indistinguishable from full insurance. At ρ=0.6\rho=0.6ρ=0.6 they are 4.0912 and 23.82 for μ=1\mu=1μ=1, 3.8767 and 24.25 for μ=3\mu=3μ=3, and 3.5857 and 24.86 for μ=5\mu=5μ=5. At ρ=0.9\rho=0.9ρ=0.9 they are 3.9305 and 24.14, 3.2903 and 25.51, and 2.5260 and 27.36.

At ρ=0.9\rho=0.9ρ=0.9 they are 3.3054 and 25.47, 1.2894 and 31.00, and −0.3456-0.3456−0.3456 and 37.63.

  • Magnitude of precautionary saving: the interest rate falls and the saving rate rises monotonically in σ\sigmaσ, ρ\rhoρ and μ\muμ. For moderate values the saving rate rises by at most about three points. With high variability, persistence and risk aversion it rises by up to seven points (31.00 against 23.67), and in the extreme case σ=0.4\sigma=0.4σ=0.4, ρ=0.9\rho=0.9ρ=0.9, μ=5\mu=5μ=5 by almost fourteen points, with a negative interest rate. A difference-stationary earnings process, the limit in which ρ\rhoρ approaches one with σ[2(1−ρ)]1/2\sigma[2(1-\rho)]^{1/2}σ[2(1−ρ)]1/2 fixed, would raise saving enormously.

  • Variabilities: consumption varies about 50 to 70 percent as much as income, saving about three times as much and assets about twice as much. Risk aversion lowers all variabilities, and consumption variability rises with persistence.

  • Distributions: all cross-section distributions are positively skewed and the fraction of liquidity-constrained households is close to zero. Inequality is ordered as in the data (consumption lowest, then net income, gross income, capital, and saving highest), but its level is too low: with μ=5\mu=5μ=5, ρ=0.6\rho=0.6ρ=0.6, σ=0.2\sigma=0.2σ=0.2 the Gini coefficients are 0.12 for net income and 0.32 for wealth, against about 0.4 and 0.8 in United States data. Median income and capital exceed 90 percent of their means, against about 80 percent for household income in the data.

The saving results can be related to the concepts of Kimball (1990). For the preferences used here, relative prudence and the equivalent precautionary premium are:

RP=μ+1,EPP=RP (σc)22(27)RP=\mu+1,\qquad EPP=RP\,\frac{(\sigma_c)^2}{2} \tag{27}RP=μ+1,EPP=RP2(σc​)2​(27)

where σc\sigma_cσc​ is the coefficient of variation of consumption. Higher σ\sigmaσ or ρ\rhoρ shifts Ea(r)Ea(r)Ea(r) to the right and raises σc\sigma_cσc​, and higher μ\muμ shifts the curve and raises RPRPRP directly. The importance of asset trading is measured with the approximate welfare loss from consumption variability, as a fraction of average consumption:

μσc22(28)\frac{\mu\sigma_c^2}{2} \tag{28}2μσc2​​(28)

A consumer who could not trade, held the per capita capital stock forever and consumed ct=rk+wltc_t=rk+wl_tct​=rk+wlt​ would have:

σc=σ1+rk/w=σ1+αr(1−α)(r+δ)(29)\sigma_c=\frac{\sigma}{1+rk/w}=\frac{\sigma}{1+\dfrac{\alpha r}{(1-\alpha)(r+\delta)}} \tag{29}σc​=1+rk/wσ​=1+(1−α)(r+δ)αr​σ​(29)

which uses the Cobb-Douglas relation k/w=α/[(r+δ)(1−α)]k/w=\alpha/[(r+\delta)(1-\alpha)]k/w=α/[(r+δ)(1−α)]. For μ=3\mu=3μ=3, σ=0.4\sigma=0.4σ=0.4, ρ=0.6\rho=0.6ρ=0.6 this gives σc=0.35\sigma_c=0.35σc​=0.35, while the equilibrium value is 0.17. Optimal accumulation and decumulation of assets thus cuts consumption variability in half, a welfare benefit of about 14 percent of per capita consumption, which the paper states as about 8 percent of per capita output. This contrasts with representative agent models, in which the gains from smoothing are small (Cochrane 1989). Finally, because earnings are approximately log-normal, the ratio of median to mean earnings is governed by σ\sigmaσ alone:

medianmean≅exp⁡(−σ22)(30)\frac{\text{median}}{\text{mean}}\cong\exp\left(-\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right) \tag{30}meanmedian​≅exp(−2σ2​)(30)

which is 0.98 for σ=0.2\sigma=0.2σ=0.2 and 0.92 for σ=0.4\sigma=0.4σ=0.4, so the model cannot reproduce the skewness of the data without much larger earnings dispersion.

This is the objective of one household in the income fluctuation problem. The term ctc_tct​ is consumption in period ttt, UUU is the period utility function (strictly increasing and strictly concave), β\betaβ is the utility discount factor with 0<β<10<\beta<10<β<1, and E0E_0E0​ is the expectation over the household's own future labor endowment shocks, conditional on what is known at date 000. Preferences are time separable and of the expected utility type, so the same concavity of UUU governs risk aversion and the desire to smooth consumption over time.

The discount factor is usually restated as the rate of time preference λ\lambdaλ:

The infinite horizon matters because it is what makes average assets explode as rrr approaches λ\lambdaλ (equations (13) and (14)). With the calibrated value β=0.96\beta=0.96β=0.96 one gets λ≈0.0417\lambda\approx0.0417λ≈0.0417, the full insurance interest rate of equation (19). The objective is maximized subject to equation (2) and is written recursively in equation (7).

This is the equilibrium condition of the model: the capital market clears in the steady state. On the left, K(r)K(r)K(r) is the capital firms want to rent at interest rate rrr, from equation (16) or (17). On the right, Ea(r)Ea(r)Ea(r) is the per capita wealth households want to hold at that rrr; it is the function EawEa_wEaw​ of equation (12) evaluated at the wage w=ω(r)w=\omega(r)w=ω(r) that is consistent with the same rrr. Capital is the only asset in positive net supply, so household wealth must equal the capital stock; loans between households cancel in the aggregate.

It is one equation in one unknown, rrr. Goods market clearing then holds by Walras' law, and the labor market clears because labor is supplied inelastically. Existence follows from continuity: for rrr near λ\lambdaλ the right side is arbitrarily large while the left side is finite, and for low rrr the right side is near −ϕ≤0-\phi\leq0−ϕ≤0 while the left side is large, so the curves cross at some r<λr<\lambdar<λ. Uniqueness is not guaranteed because Ea(r)Ea(r)Ea(r) need not be monotone. This condition is what the bisection algorithm solves, and it is what turns the partial equilibrium fact that assets explode near λ\lambdaλ into the general equilibrium result that rrr settles below λ\lambdaλ by an amount that depends on the elasticity of K(r)K(r)K(r).

This is the period utility function of the quantitative model, constant relative risk aversion (isoelastic). The single parameter μ>0\mu>0μ>0 is the coefficient of relative risk aversion and, because preferences are time separable, also the inverse of the elasticity of intertemporal substitution. Subtracting one in the numerator does not change behaviour; it makes the limit as μ\muμ goes to one well defined, and that limit is logarithmic utility.

lim⁡μ→1c1−μ−11−μ=log⁡c\lim_{\mu\to1}\frac{c^{1-\mu}-1}{1-\mu}=\log cμ→1lim​1−μc1−μ−1​=logc

The form buys several things used in the note. Relative risk aversion is bounded, the key condition for a bounded support and a stationary distribution when r<λr<\lambdar<λ (it rules out the negative exponential case mentioned before equation (12)). Marginal utility is unbounded at zero, so ct≥0c_t\geq0ct​≥0 never binds, and it is convex, so the classical precautionary motive is present with relative prudence μ+1\mu+1μ+1 (equation (27)). Homogeneity makes the problem scale with the wage when b=0b=0b=0, and it is what allows balanced growth in equation (21). The values μ∈{1,3,5}\mu\in\{1,3,5\}μ∈{1,3,5} span the range commonly used; a higher μ\muμ raises both the aversion to consumption fluctuations and the strength of the precautionary motive, and the model cannot separate the two.

This is the assumed process for idiosyncratic labor endowments (equivalently earnings, since the wage is constant) in the quantitative model. The log endowment is a first-order autoregression with persistence ρ\rhoρ and a standard normal innovation ϵt\epsilon_tϵt​. The innovation is scaled by σ(1−ρ2)1/2\sigma(1-\rho^2)^{1/2}σ(1−ρ2)1/2 so that σ\sigmaσ is the unconditional standard deviation of the log endowment whatever the value of ρ\rhoρ. c.v.=(eσ2−1)1/2,which is 0.202 for σ=0.2 and 0.417 for σ=0.4\text{c.v.}=\left(e^{\sigma^2}-1\right)^{1/2},\qquad\text{which is }0.202\text{ for }\sigma=0.2\text{ and }0.417\text{ for }\sigma=0.4c.v.=(eσ2−1)1/2,which is 0.202 for σ=0.2 and 0.417 for σ=0.4

Shocks are independent across households, so there is no aggregate risk. The process is trend stationary: a shock decays at rate ρ\rhoρ per year. Because the current shock now helps predict future earnings, it becomes a state variable in addition to total resources, and the i.i.d. analysis of equations (5) to (15) is the special case ρ=0\rho=0ρ=0. The continuous process is replaced by a seven-state Markov chain for computation. The values of σ\sigmaσ and ρ\rhoρ are taken from panel data on earnings, using equation (26) to convert the dispersion of earnings growth into the dispersion of the level.

mean(x)=E[elog⁡x]=em+σ2/2\text{mean}(x)=E\left[e^{\log x}\right]=e^{m+\sigma^2/2}mean(x)=E[elogx]=em+σ2/2

Take the ratio; the location parameter cancels.

medianmean=emem+σ2/2=exp⁡(−σ22)\frac{\text{median}}{\text{mean}}=\frac{e^{m}}{e^{m+\sigma^2/2}}=\exp\left(-\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)meanmedian​=em+σ2/2em​=exp(−2σ2​)

The relation is exact for a log-normal variable when σ\sigmaσ is the standard deviation of the log; the approximation sign reflects that the model's earnings follow a seven-state chain that is only approximately log-normal, and that σ\sigmaσ is loosely called the coefficient of variation. Numerically:

exp⁡(−0.02)=0.980,exp⁡(−0.08)=0.923\exp(-0.02)=0.980,\qquad\exp(-0.08)=0.923exp(−0.02)=0.980,exp(−0.08)=0.923

To reach the ratio of about 0.8 seen in household income data one would need σ=(−2log⁡0.8)1/2≈0.67\sigma=(-2\log0.8)^{1/2}\approx0.67σ=(−2log0.8)1/2≈0.67, far above the calibrated range. The same expansion explains the skewness measure used in the note: mean minus median over standard deviation is approximately σ/2\sigma/2σ/2 for a log-normal variable.
